PART 1 - Introduction
Agriculture is at the heart of our daily lives. Farmers produce high quality, safe food, they look
after the natural landscape, help tackle climate change and preserve the vitality of our
countryside. The CAP enables European farmers to deliver benefits for the whole society, by
ensuring a supply of high-quality affordable food.
Strategic planning and programming is the cornerstone of the Commission’s performance
management framework. The Commission’s strategic plan for 2025-2029 translates the
political priorities set in the Political Guidelines of President von der Leyen into general
objectives. This process ensures institutional coherence, enhances accountability, and aligns the
actions of all Commission services with the strategic vision of the mandate.
Within this framework, each Commission service has developed a strategic outlook for
2025-2029 in the Management plan 2025. This outlook defines a set of multiannual
objectives and indicators to measure progress towards their achievement. These will be used
for planning and reporting on performance throughout the period.
The 2026 management plan sets out what DG for Agriculture and Rural Development
(DG AGRI) intends to deliver this year to contribute to these multiannual objectives (part 2). It
also describes how DG AGRI will contribute to the common objective of building a modern and
sustainable public administration (part 3). The main outputs with their indicators and targets
are presented in Annexes 1 and 2.
The chart below illustrates the performance framework for DG AGRI.

PART 2 - Delivering on the Commission’s
priorities in 2026 (1)
General objective 1: A new plan for Europe’s sustainable
prosperity and competitiveness
Specific Objective 1.1: Strengthen the attractiveness of the agri-food
sector for new and current generations and improve its long-term
sustainable competitiveness
During 2026, DG AGRI will continue work on both implementing the Vision for Agriculture and
Food, and the Simpler and Faster Europe Communication, enhancing farm competitiveness,
whilst delivering on the overarching priority of simplification and reduction of the
administrative burden. Following the approval by the co-legislators of the changes to the
CAP basic legislation for 2023-2027 (Omnibus III), further simplification of secondary
legislation is being prepared and will be adopted in January 2026.
The Commission will review the unfair trading practices Directive. This may increase compliance
efforts for some operators but is expected to reduce overall transaction and legal costs through
clearer rules and better enforcement mechanisms.
In 2026, DG AGRI is planning the organisation of two Implementation Dialogues with
stakeholders (one planned for Q1/2026). The results and actions related to implementation,
simplification and enforcement will be part of the Annual Progress Report to the EP and the
Council.
In 2026, DG AGRI will continue preparations for the transition to the 2028-2034 MFF and CAP
legal framework, whilst optimising the implementation of the current CAP 2023-2027
framework. It will start working on the implementation of
the future CAP and, in particular, it will prepare CAP
national recommendations in support of the preparation
of Member States’ national plans to ensure the
appropriate level of ambition and coherence of the CAP
implementation across Member States. DG AGRI will
continue providing feedback on the implementation of
current CAP plans. This will include continuous dialogue
and engagement with stakeholders, Member States and
the European Parliament. © European Union
Building on the report of the Strategic Dialogue on the Future of EU Agriculture (2), the
Commission intends to maintain active collaboration with the members of the European Board

on Agriculture and Food (EBAF). Dedicated meetings will be organised and chaired by
Commissioner Hansen to discuss topics such as the livestock strategy and the international
dimensions of the Vision for Agriculture and Food. The forthcoming Food Dialogue will bring
together actors across the food system to address issues such as competitiveness and
procurement.
As announced in the Vision for Agriculture and Food, DG AGRI will elaborate a comprehensive
plan for a more self-sufficient and sustainable EU protein system by 2026. The Commission
will also work on a livestock strategy to foster the competitiveness, resilience and
sustainability of the EU livestock sector and agri-food chain. The plan for the protein sector
and the livestock workstream will be coordinated for synergies to ensure consistency. The
Commission will also develop the on-farm sustainability compass work programme,
including a multistakeholder workshop and sectoral dialogues supported by the AGRI-EIB fi-
compass study.
Following the adoption of the Strategy for Generational Renewal in Agriculture in October
2025, the Commission will implement the actions of therein, notably the Pilot Project study on
the EU Observatory on Farmland, with its initial phase expected to be concluded by September
2026. and the Women in Farming Platform. This platform will aim to attract more women to
agriculture, promote equal opportunities, exchange of experiences and mentoring, recognising
women’s key role in the future of farming and rural development. It will serve as a forum to
discuss and exchange good practices. The Generational Renewal Strategy will likewise aim at
supporting the design and implementation of dedicated financial instruments for young
farmers, improving the conditions offered to young farmers, and backing up their efforts in
developing better business proposals. This will also address the initiation of financial products
and opportunities under other policies with support from the EIB, EIF or other implementing
partners.
Following the adoption of the “wine package” by the Council and the European Parliament, the
Commission will adopt the secondary legislation necessary for its implementation. In 2026, the
Commission will also continue the work on possible Union rules enhancing the development of
the EU cider sector. An update of the marketing standards for fruit and vegetables and
oenological practices in line with international developments will take place in 2026. Moreover,
considering that the amended Directive (3) on fruit juices will be applied by Member States from
June 2026, the Commission will adopt a delegated regulation allowing for some technological
adjustments necessary to produce reduced-sugar fruit juices.
As announced by President von der Leyen in her speech on the State of the European Union, the
“Buy European Food Campaign” will promote EU food quality and sustainability, connecting
consumers with local farmers.

Specific Objective 1.2: Support research and innovation (R&I) and
enhance the access and use of R&I, knowledge, digitalisation and
skills
Digitalisation, technological tools as well as research and innovation (R&I) are major enablers
to foster the transition to a more competitive, resilient and sustainable agriculture and forestry,
and to support the viability of rural areas.
DG AGRI supports the uptake of new technologies and tools bringing benefits to farmers
and public administration, such as the Area Monitoring System, Land Parcel Identification
System and Geospatial Aid Application and the use of AI. It will
continue to implement the European Innovation Partnership for
Agricultural Productivity and Sustainability (EIP-AGRI) and the
Agricultural Knowledge and Innovation System (AKIS). DG AGRI will
also closely follow the various Commission legislative initiatives on
data and digital (i.e. Common European Agricultural Data Space,
'Interoperable Europe Portal'). DG AGRI will thus ensure coordination
of digitalisation and data technologies in the agricultural sector,
© European Union
enhancing market orientation and increasing the competitiveness of
farmers.
Since 2023, the mandatory Area Monitoring System (AMS), an element of the Integrated
Administration and Control system (IACS) uses automatised, AI based interpretation of satellite
imagery and data of equivalent value (e.g. geotagged photos and drones) for monitoring
performance of CAP support. This novelty pushed Member States’ administration to integrate
working methods using new technologies into their daily administration and governance of CAP
support.
In 2026, Horizon Europe Cluster 6 will include 44 new projects designed to address knowledge
and innovation gaps and develop new opportunities in thematic areas such as crop and animal
health, water management, sustainable livestock and forestry, boosting EU advisory capacities
for farmers. Furthermore, under the EU Mission ‘A Soil Deal for Europe’, 20 new Mission Soil
living labs will begin operating and a call for proposals will be launched in 2026 for another 20
to start in 2027. In total, 17 new R&I projects on soil health will start under the Mission Soil.
In the year ahead, a new EU strategic approach to R&I to improve the competitiveness of
agriculture, forestry and rural areas will be prepared, followed by the fourth edition of the EU
AgriResearch Conference. The new strategic approach will revamp the existing strategic
approach dating from 2016, taking stock of achievements and framing current and future
challenges and opportunities for agricultural R&I towards 2040.
DG AGRI will continue to support the EU CAP Network, a key platform involving a broad range
of stakeholders that has become a major facilitator for knowledge exchanges, covering all
aspects of the CAP Strategic Plans. In the framework of CAP support and rural broadband
infrastructure deployment, DG AGRI will continue to manage the contract for the Support
Facility of the Broadband Competence Offices (BCO) Network.
7

General objective 3: Supporting people, strengthening our
societies and our social model
Specific Objective 3.1: Building stronger connections between people
and food and ensuring fair working and living conditions in attractive
rural areas
Building stronger connections between people and food and ensuring fair working and living
conditions in attractive rural areas are key objectives of the Vision for Agriculture and Food. To
deliver on this objective, DG AGRI will continue acting as the coordinator of the implementation
of the EU Rural action plan (30 actions), as well as a facilitator for the Rural Pact, co-
leading with DG REGIO.
The first significant number of projects relating to investments in services and infrastructure in
rural areas will be finalised by 2026.
The Rural Development Programmes 2014-2022 will be closed in 2026.
In addition, DG AGRI will support LEADER through workshops, communication material and
technical support. The Local Action Groups (LAGs) selected under the CAP Strategic Plans (CSPs)
for the 2023-2027 period will continue implementing Local Development Strategies and
complete a significant number of projects. Furthermore, the Commission will launch a study on
the impact of the social conditionality mechanism on workers’ conditions and functioning of the
system of penalties as requested by the co-legislators.
Providing clear and simple rules for producers and their products is also an important part of
the work ahead in 2026. In that regard, the Commission will provide further guidance on
existing rules concerning mixing of olive oil and engage with Member States to further improve
their respective control and traceability systems such as surveys, technical guidance, and
exchange of best practices. Subject to amendments of the International Olive oil Council (IOC)
trade standard in 2026, the Commission may adapt the EU marketing standards for olive oil to
fulfil its international commitments.
General objective 4: Sustaining our quality of life: food
security, water and nature
Specific Objective 4.1: Help farmers earn a fair and sufficient income,
including through reinforcing the position of farmers in the food chain
Following the publication of the evaluation in 2025, the Commission will propose a revision of
Directive (EU) 2019/633 on unfair trading practices (UTP Directive). The revision will
consider further adjustments to strengthen and harmonise enforcement and to tackle the ‘fear
factor’ that prevents farmers and small suppliers from reporting when they have been
subjected to unfair trading practices. It will also look into improving the Directive’s
effectiveness in supporting the economic viability of farmers and smaller suppliers. In
8

particular, the Commission will examine options related to the principle that farmers should not
be forced to systematically sell below their production costs.
The Commission will continue to facilitate the network meetings and exchanges between the
UTP enforcement authorities. For example, following the adoption of the proposal on
cooperation between authorities responsible for enforcing the UTP Directive, the Commission
will start implementing an information system to support exchanges among the enforcement
authorities and prepare a Commission Implementing Regulation establishing standard forms
for such communications.
After the adoption of the targeted amendment of the Common Market Organisation (CMO)
Regulation on strengthening the position of farmers in the food chain, the Commission will start
working on the Commission Implementing Regulation to further specify conditions for the use
of optional terms for commercial modalities, such as ‘fair’, ‘equitable’ and ‘short supply chain’.
The Commission will continue the Market Observatories for different sectors (grains, sugar,
olive oil, milk, meats, fruit and vegetables and wine) and agricultural inputs (fertilisers) which
contribute to enhancing market information and transparency. Building on such market
information, the Agri Food Chain Observatory (AFCO) will look at costs of the main stages of
the food supply chain and at the distribution of margins and value added along the chain, with
the objective of supporting evidence-based discussion between actors along the food supply
chain and with the Commission.
The Commission will reinforce its efforts to facilitate cooperation between financial institutions
(banks and guarantee funds), EAFRD managing authorities and young farmers to respond to
improve access to finance and better incomes.
Specific Objective 4.2: Boost the resilience of the agri-food sector and
improve farmers’ contribution to food security and their ability to
cope with risks and crises
In 2026, the Commission will continue its efforts regarding support instruments that increase
farm resilience. It will further promote the uptake of risk management tools in the CAP
Strategic Plans by facilitating the implementation of the new flexibilities offered in the CAP
simplification package (Omnibus III), along with the new tool for crisis payments, included in the
same package. The Commission will in particular focus on how risk management tools, crisis
payments, investments in prevention of and restoration of agricultural production potential
after natural disasters and other relevant tools together can contribute to better risk
management to increase farm level resilience. DG AGRI, under its fi-compass technical
assistance programme, is undertaking a study with the EIB on the feasibility and design of EU
agricultural catastrophe risk financing instruments, with specific focus on the development of
relevant insurance scheme(s) for EU farmers.
To ensure a sufficient and varied supply of safe, nutritious, affordable and sustainable food to
EU citizens at all times, including in time of crises, the expert group on the European Food
Security Crisis preparedness and response Mechanism (EFSCM) meets on a regular basis
to step up levels of preparedness in the EU. In 2026, this will include assessing the options of
public-private cooperation on stockpiling of agri-food products as a preparedness measure. In
9

the event of a crisis, this group is convened on an ad-hoc basis to discuss and resolve problems
and bottlenecks at an early stage.
The proposed revision of the Common Market Organisation (CMO) Regulation, tabled in the
context of the post-2027 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), includes provisions for
further strengthening resilience, in line with the EU Preparedness Union and EU Stockpiling
Strategies. It introduces a new chapter on the availability of agricultural supplies in crises,
requiring Member States to develop national food security plans. Where reserves are created,
those must operate at market prices and minimise market distortions. While the EFSCM will be
reinforced as the EU’s coordination platform on food security, the Commission will focus on
ensuring effective coordination, data exchange and solidarity mechanisms across the Union.
Dedicated focus meetings within the EFSCM will help shaping the ongoing discussion with the
co-legislators.
The Commission will continue to propose and adopt the necessary market measures and
exceptional measures if this proves necessary. It will also, in 2026, prepare the report required
every three years by the CMO Regulation on the application of exceptional measures.
Specific Objective 4.3: Supporting an agri-food sector that enhances
climate action, ecosystem services provision, conservation and
restoration of biodiversity and natural resources
In 2026, DG AGRI will continue to steer the CAP support to the environment and climate
objectives, to achieve the targets agreed under the CAP Strategic Plans. In particular, the CAP
green architecture, such as conditionality, eco-schemes, agro-environment-climate
commitments or green investments, will continue to aid delivery of the relevant targets.
As foreseen in the Vision for Agriculture and Food, DG AGRI supports the objectives of the
Water Resilience Strategy. In this context, DG AGRI will continue to support Member States
and stakeholders to maximise the use of CAP Strategic Plans for water resilience through
knowledge sharing and innovative solutions promoted by the EU CAP Network, including
through the organisation of a major conference on “Innovative solutions for water resilience in
agriculture’ in May 2026.
In the area of climate change mitigation, DG AGRI continues identifying and promoting best
practices to reduce agricultural greenhouse gas emissions in close cooperation with Member
States. DG AGRI supports various initiatives (such as establishing the certification
methodologies for carbon farming activities under the CRCF framework (4).
In the area of organics, a number of simplification-related activities in 2026 aim to render the
sector more competitive. DG AGRI will engage with the co-legislators on the proposed
amendment of the organics basic act scheduled for adoption towards the end of 2026.
DG AGRI’s roadmap for other simplification projects will be rolled out over the course of 2026,
to further unlock the potential of the EU organic sector and strengthen its contribution to
sustainable agriculture.
(4) Carbon Removal Certification Framework
10

In the context of the review of the EU Forest Strategy for 2030, DG AGRI (co-leading with
DG CLIMA and DG ENV) will prepare a report to evaluate progress in the implementation of the
strategy actions at EU level as well as at Member States level (national, regional and local).
General objective 6: A global Europe: Leveraging our power
and partnerships
Specific Objective 6.1: Promote the EU’s strategic autonomy, fairer
competition in global agri-food trade and foster international
dialogue
In the international sphere, DG AGRI will continue to work in support of a thriving, competitive
and resilient agri-food sector in times of geopolitical turbulence. Recent years have brought
multiple overlapping crises, such as increasingly frequent extreme climatic events, Russia’s war
of aggression against Ukraine, the Middle East crisis, and an increasingly complex and
unpredictable trade environment.
Against that background, DG AGRI will continue to support efforts to improve global food
security and promote the EU’s strategic autonomy through international agri-food trade and
multilateral co-operation in agriculture.
Strengthening the resilience of the global food system will remain a key objective in all our
bilateral and multilateral engagements, notably by promoting a stronger implementation of
internationally agreed commitments and by encouraging partners to increase their ambition in
the area of sustainable food systems. In line with the Vision on Agriculture and Food, DG AGRI
will work towards ensuring that the most hazardous pesticides banned in the EU for health and
environmental reasons are not allowed back to the EU through imported products. DG AGRI will
continue to represent the agricultural interests of the EU in international and multilateral fora,
from the WTO to the FAO, G7/G20 and OECD. In particular, DG AGRI will maintain its active
engagement with the WTO in view of its 14th Ministerial Conference (MC14) scheduled for 26-
29 March 2026 in Cameroon.
The emphasis is not only on negotiation but also on implementation and enforcement of
bilateral trade agreements. DG AGRI will therefore continue to pursue negotiations as well as
have a robust implementation agenda for the EU’s international agreements. A committed
enforcement policy reaps the benefits of our Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), either by fulfilling
the opportunities for exports, a reduction in technical barriers faced by companies, or a more
efficient legal protection of geographical indications (GIs), and monitoring of safeguards. This
will be complemented by reinforcing and where possible developing new agrifood policy
partnership dialogues with key bilateral partners, in line with the Vision for Agriculture and
Food. Along similar lines, the Commission will continue to represent the European Union in the
International Commodity Bodies (5) as well as coordinate the positions of the Member States
members of the international wine organisation (OIV). The Commission contributes to the work
(5) International Sugar Organisation (ISO), International Grains Council (IGC) and International Olive Council (IOC)
11

of the Agricultural Market Information System (AMIS), an inter-agency platform to enhance
food market transparency and policy response for food security.
In line with the Vision, the Commission will be more assertive in promoting and defending
strategically the exports of EU products, ensuring that third countries will benefit from the
implementation of trade facilitation measures, such as prelisting, provided that they also apply
similar measures in relation to the EU.
In 2026, the Commission will continue to update rules on trade mechanisms, to align them
with the agreements with third countries, and to adapt them to ensure proper trade
management.
DG AGRI will continue providing advice and assistance to enlargement countries on CAP
policy and overall acquis alignment obligations. DG AGRI will be fully engaged in the different
steps of the enlargement negotiations for the chapter on agriculture and rural development. DG
AGRI will also continue implementing pre-accession assistance programmes for rural
development (IPARD III) in the beneficiary countries.
In 2026, the Commission will adjust several acts regarding the incremental roll-over of a major
trade facilitation measure by 2030 concerning the digitalisation of agricultural non-custom
procedures (namely export and import licences) to accommodate the further developments of
ELAN (6) related to certificates of conformity.
As recognised in the Vision for Agriculture and Food, the EU’s agri-food promotion policy is a
key tool to support the competitiveness of the sector, offering opportunities to consolidate,
develop and diversify EU export markets. The policy’s main focus is to co-finance promotion
campaigns. In addition, the Commission’s own initiatives for agri-food promotion include high-
level missions, EU pavilions at international trade fairs and communication campaigns in
markets with major growth potential. It also funds market entry handbooks to help EU agri-
food exporters tap into new markets.

PART 3. A modern and sustainable public
administration: outputs in 2026 (7)
The internal control framework supports sound management and decision-making. In particular,
it ensures that risks to the achievement of objectives are addressed and reduced to acceptable
levels through cost-effective controls.
The Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development (DG AGRI) has established an
internal control system tailored to its particular characteristics and circumstances. The effective
functioning of this internal control system will be assessed on an ongoing basis throughout the
year and will be subject to an annual assessment covering all internal control principles.
A. Human resource management
In 2026, the DG AGRI Human Resources (HR) Correspondent Team will tackle new challenges
and adapt to changes in key HR areas. Priorities for the year will be for instance to monitor
DG AGRI’s job quota, ensure the optimal use of resources in line with policy and operational
priorities, adapt recruitment procedures, ensure optimal use of talent or support staff’s
professional development, as well as to rapidly fill vacant senior management positions. The
female share of middle management positions is increasing (from 54% in 2024 to 56,4% in
2025).
Staff engagement as well as communication activities remain a central aspect of HR policy.
Based on the upcoming results of the 2025 Staff Survey, DG AGRI intends to formulate a new
follow-up action plan. Furthermore, DG AGRI’s Equality Mainstreaming Work Plan will continue
to support equality and inclusion in all HR processes.
B. Digital transformation and data management
Digital transformation: DG AGRI takes action to achieve each of the strategic objectives of
the European Commission Corporate Digital Strategy.
Digital culture – DG AGRI promotes digital upskilling through networks, working groups,
presentations and training material, and the Data corner on the AGRI intranet. The DG AGRI
Data Upskill Strategy includes actions to help colleagues learn to access, understand and
analyse agricultural data. A DG AGRI AI strategy has been established, resulting in the inclusion
of Artificial Intelligence domain in mandate of the DG AGRI Data and AI Governance Board and
the transition of the DG AGRI Data Management Working Group into the DG AGRI Data and AI
Network which is being leveraged to identify potential AI use cases (first ones identified are the
AI agents on PMEF Databot, CAP plans comparison and AGRI Wiki).
(7) Annex 2 provides more details on other envisaged outputs for 2026 for the specific objectives (page 31 ff).
13

Digital-ready EU policymaking - DG AGRI reminds its staff to include IT requirements of
digital relevance in its IT Master Plan, whenever planning a new piece of legislation, by referring
to the Better Regulation guidelines and more specifically tool #28 on Digital-ready
policymaking. In this regard, the Unit responsible for “Data Governance” supports and provides
guidance to policy officers to implement the Digital-ready-Policy-Making framework.
Business transformation – DG AGRI develops and improves digital tools (8) with a view to
further automating business processes, preparing for the integration with other Commission
systems (including AI tools), or enabling digital transformation.
Seamless digital environment – DG AGRI information systems consistently use several of
the Reusable Solutions Platform modules. DG AGRI re-uses systems/modules developed by
other DGs and co-develops Compass Corporate and SFC2021. Annual DG AGRI IT surveys are
launched to gather input on user satisfaction and possible ideas for improvements in relation to
DG AGRI Information Systems.
DG AGRI commits to promote a secure deployment of new cloud workloads using the new EC
Cloud Security Controls Baseline (CSCB), the EC Managed Landing Zone and the
recommendations of the Cloud Council.
Green, secure and resilient infrastructure - All DG AGRI Information Systems have a
Security Plan based on the new ITSRM (9) methodology. All risk assessments are being migrated
to the GovSec tool of DIGIT.S. Departmental and system controls are attested in the
Governance-Risk-Compliance (GRC) tool every year. For synergies and efficiencies, DG AGRI
uses the c‑LISO service provided by DG DIGIT.
As agreed with the C-LISO, DG AGRI will implement the actions presented in the Commission’s
Cybersecurity Plan 2025-2026, relevant to the service.
Data management: DG AGRI’s rolling Data and AI Action Plan encompasses the activities
identified along the key four areas:
- Data Management: Continued assessment of data policies fulfilment in DG AGRI IT systems
and further improvement of the umbrella data warehouse of DG AGRI (AGRIVIEW), by
developing new data flows (such as DIOB – Data on Intervention and beneficiaries) and
identifying data gaps. Continuation of the DEPINT project on data interoperability to
seamlessly integrate agricultural data from European and national-level systems, and the
Common Agricultural Data Space to foster a single market for agricultural data.
- Ownership and responsibilities: Through established allocation of responsibilities, including
data stewardship, in the context of the PMEF (Performance and Monitoring Evaluation
Framework of the CAP), DG AGRI will deliver value in the coordination of data quality checks
and evidence-based analysis.
- Data Quality: investments will continue in automating data retrieval and processing from
external sources including automated data quality checks to guarantee data consistency.
- Data skills: DG AGRI will carry out training on Data/AI tools and technologies.
(8) Compass Corporate, Farm Sustainability Data Network (FSDN), Agri-food data portal, conversion
(9) IT Security and Risk Management
14

The 2025 baseline for the maturity level in implementing corporate data policies is either
“established” (data quality, data management, data ownership and responsibilities) or
“advanced” (data skills). For 2026, DG AGRI intends to keep the maturity level in implementing
corporate data policies at least at “established” for data quality and data ownership, and
“advanced” for data skills. DG AGRI also envisages to reach the level of “advanced” for data
management.
Data Protection: To maintain a complete overview of the processing of personal data in the
DG, DG AGRI will carry out the yearly data protection inventory. The Data Protection Coordinator
will continue to advise DG AGRI staff to ensure the correct implementation of the EU Data
Protection Regulation (10). General and targeted training on data protection compliance will
continue to be provided, and awareness-raising campaigns will be conducted.
C. Sound financial management
Assurance and audit
In 2026, with the implementation of the CAP 2023-2027 fully on track (representing 77% of
the shared management expenditure in 2024), DG AGRI audits will mainly focus on the
functioning of the governance systems (11) designed and set up by the Member States
according to their CAP Strategic Plans and in line with the relevant basic acts. Where relevant,
and considering the current situation in terms of risk, audits will also cover measures with
expenditure outside the CAP Strategic Plans. As regards indirect management, DG AGRI will
continue to audit the instrument for pre-accession assistance in rural development (IPARD)
expenditure entrusted to the beneficiary countries in accordance with the applicable framework
and sectoral agreements.
In 2026, DG AGRI will begin implementing its Multi-Annual Work Programme for 2026-
2027 (including 99 audit missions and 60 desk audits), based on DG AGRI’s updated
Assurance and Audit strategy approved in 2025. This update is based on the experience gained
from the first two years of implementation of the CAP 2023 to 2027. Based on an analysis of
the main risks, the Strategy determines the audit and capacity building means to achieve the
DG’s assurance objectives. In the context of shared management, the Strategy recalls the
principles that DG AGRI audits are risk-based systems audits, that the assurance building
mainly rests on existing governance bodies in the Member States, and that it follows the
principle of the single audit approach.
In December 2025, the co-legislators adopted the CAP “simplification package” (Omnibus III),
proposed by the Commission in May 2025. Among other things, the package provides for the
discontinuation of the annual performance clearance, in light of experience gained from the

first annual performance clearance exercise, which demonstrated that the administrative
burden for Member States is disproportionate.
DG AGRI will provide assurance to the Director-General on the relevant expenditure incurred
during the year, in relation to the functioning of the Member States’ governance systems and
performance for expenditure under the CAP Strategic Plans and to the legality and regularity
for expenditure outside the CAP Strategic Plans. As regards 2026, the share of low-risk
expenditure should stay in the range of 66% of the total relevant expenditure. The baseline of
66% corresponds to the annual average of low-risk expenditure between financial years 2020
and 2024.
Financial management
In the framework of the Draft Budget exercise, DG AGRI will request appropriations for the
financing of the CAP in 2027, both for EAGF and EAFRD. DG AGRI will closely follow up the
execution of the 2026 budget via three “révisions conjoncturelles” of the EAGF.
DG AGRI will continue ensuring and promoting sound and efficient management of the financial
resources under direct, indirect and shared management (in particular regarding the respect of
accurate and timely payments and closure of the Rural Development programmes).
As regards accounting, the focus will be on preparing and ensuring the accuracy and reliability
of the general accounts of DG AGRI with the aim of receiving a positive Declaration of
Assurance from the European Court of Auditors.
Under the lead of DG BUDG, HR and SG, DG AGRI will contribute to the cost-benefit analysis
(CBA) for the direct programme implementation 2028-2034.
D. Fraud risk management
Based on OLAF Final Reports on investigations, DG AGRI audits, and other suitable sources, the
fraud risk within CAP expenditure is monitored as an ongoing activity. Should new fraud
patterns emerge, they will be brought to the attention of the competent authorities and Paying
Agencies in the Member States as well as to DG AGRI staff as appropriate.
In 2026, the action plan included in DG AGRI Anti-Fraud Strategy (12) will be implemented with
the following actions:
- the internal procedure for the handling of allegations of fraud and other irregularities, and
of OLAF/EPPO cases will be updated as necessary;
- the new DG AGRI Anti-Fraud Strategy will be prepared in 2026 as agreed with OLAF so to
replace the one in place which was adopted in 2020;
- seminars will be organised in presence for the Member States and the Paying Agencies
depending on requests received (Action 2 in the current DG AGRI AFS);
- training events will be provided for all staff of DG AGRI on fraud detection and prevention
depending on requests received (Action 4 in the current DG AGRI AFS);

- the follow-up of OLAF’s financial recommendations will be closely monitored along the
procedures already developed (Actions 3 and 5 in the current DG AGRI AFS).
DG AGRI will continue to contribute to all relevant actions included in the 2023 Commission
anti-fraud strategy Action Plan (in particular Actions 11a, 12, 14, 15, 18, 19b and 36).
E. Sound environmental management
Mission requests will be carefully monitored, in particular those involving more than three staff
members. In line with the new Mission Guide, more sustainable ways of travelling will be
promoted with a view to further reducing CO2 emissions (baseline: 1 506,72 t in 2019).
To improve IT greening, an awareness campaign will encourage colleagues to switch off their
laptops and docking stations when they leave the office. DG AGRI will continue to support
corporate actions, such as the Walking Challenge, VeloMai and the energy-saving initiatives in
the summer and at year-end. DG AGRI will also pursue the organisation of the successful
clothes’ swaps events, which encourage colleagues to re-use and exchange clothes. Finally, a
group of enthusiastic volunteers will continue to take care of AGRI’s potager in the L130
courtyard.
